entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

The tours are built and committed, but they have never been run in a browser. The Playwright session was never run: first the disk dropped to about 2 GB free (your stop threshold), then the heavy-lock queue was over 20 jobs, and then the usage-window stop came. The final typecheck re-run is still queued behind the lock.

**Branch:** `feature/guided-first-run-tours` in `/opt/nxeon-wt-tours`, one commit, `e913fcdd00`, pushed by the hook. Progress note: `/root/agent-notes/tours.md`.

**What it does**
- A tour opens by itself the first time a customer opens a ready dashboard: dimmed page, spotlight, pulsing ring, animated pointer, step card.
- It shows once per service per user, not per server: `vps`, `hosting`, `domain`, `game:<family>`. A second Minecraft server shows nothing; a first Valheim server gets its own tour.
- Every VPS, game, hosting and domain page gets a "Take the tour" replay button. Replays skip the one-time "your server is ready" step.
- It auto-starts only when:
  - the viewer owns the service and no admin is impersonating;
  - the service is ready (server RUNNING, hosting ACTIVE, domain ACTIVE) and not behind the provisioning screen;
  - there's no progress row yet (a run interrupted by a reload resumes at its last step);
  - the user hasn't clicked "Don't show tours again";
  - the service is at most 30 days old, so long-time customers aren't greeted "your server is ready" on months-old servers.
- Impersonation: the write actions check `impersonating()` and write nothing, so admins never mark a customer's tour as seen.
- Content is built server-side from what each game can really do (one-click mods, live-applied settings, remote console, subdomain), so it never promises a feature that isn't there.
  - Dedicated tours: Minecraft, Bedrock, Valheim, Terraria, Rust, ARK, ARK:SA, CS2, Palworld. Every other game gets a generic tour that follows the same rules.
  - Plus VPS, hosting and domain tours. There's no email tour; the key is only reserved.
- The engine loads only when a tour opens and renders outside the page layout, so blurred headers can't trap it. It switches tabs by clicking the panel's own buttons.
  - A missing optional step is skipped; a missing required one shows centred with a short note.
  - It also has a focus trap, Esc and arrow keys, screen-reader announcements, reduced-motion support and a bottom sheet on phones.

**Schema:** one new model, `UserTourProgress` (`@@unique([userId, serviceKey])`), plus one back-relation line on `User`, deleted along with the user. Purely additive. Pushed only to the throwaway DB `nxeon_agt_tours`; prod needs `db push` at deploy.

**Verification so far**
- Typecheck was clean on the tree before the domain tour was added.
- 18/18 unit tests passed in `test/tours-trigger.test.ts`, also before the domain tour. They cover the trigger and persistence rules, card placement, content honesty, and a check that every id a tour points at exists in the source.
- The re-run on the final tree is queued; its result will land in `scratchpad/tours-tsc.txt`.

**Files edited outside my area** (each a one-attribute `data-tour` edit unless noted):
- Game panel: `GamePanelShell.tsx`, `GameSettingsShell.tsx`, `GameHero.tsx`, `GameSettings.tsx`, `GamePlayers.tsx`
- VPS panel: `VpsPanelShell.tsx`, `vpspanel/v2/ui.tsx`, `VpsHero.tsx` (IP chip wrapped in a layout-neutral span), `VpsPowerControls.tsx`, `VpsOverviewPanel.tsx`
- Hosting panel: `HostingPanelShell.tsx`, `HostingOverviewPanel.tsx`
- `DomainDetailShell.tsx`: also added `aria-current` to its tabs
- Mounts, a few lines each: `app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx` (both the game and VPS branches), `hosting/[id]/page.tsx`, `domains/[id]/page.tsx`
- `prisma/schema.prisma`, `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`

**Remaining, in order**
1. Re-verify: `heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-tours && npx tsc --noEmit -p . && npx tsx --test test/tours-trigger.test.ts"`
2. Run the browser test: `heavy.sh /opt/nxeon-wt-tours/.tour-e2e/run.sh`. It starts a dev server on :3115, seeds test data, runs the checks and kills the server. It covers everything in the brief, plus impersonation writing nothing and a hydration-error check. Then `rm -rf .next` and look at the screenshots in `scratchpad/tours-shots`.
3. Clean up: `sudo -u postgres dropdb nxeon_agt_tours`, remove the worktree `.env` and the untracked `.tour-e2e/` (never commit either).

**Risks**
- The look and on-screen behaviour (placement, the mobile sheet, navigation timing) are unverified until step 2 runs.
- The panel shells don't mount a shared help menu, so the replay is a button on each page. Anything else can open it with the `nx-tour:start` window event.

content.text:
I've built the guided first-run tours and committed them, but they have never been run in a browser, so how they look and behave on screen is untested. The browser test didn't run: first the disk was at about 2 GB free, then the shared lock queue was over 20 jobs long, then the main thread said to stop.

**What it does:** the first time a customer opens a newly ready server's dashboard, a walkthrough opens by itself. It dims the page, spotlights each area with a pulsing ring and a pointer, and explains what to do there. It shows once per service per customer: a second Minecraft server gets nothing, a first Valheim server gets its own tour, and a VPS has its own. Every VPS, game, hosting and domain page also gets a "Take the tour" button to replay it.

- **When it opens by itself:** only if the viewer owns the service and the service is ready. It also must not have been seen before, and the customer must not have clicked "Don't show tours again". Services older than 30 days are skipped, so existing customers aren't greeted with "your server is ready" on old servers; they can still use the replay button.
- **Admins viewing as a customer:** the tour never opens by itself and never records anything, so it isn't marked as seen for the customer.
- **Content:** written from what each game can actually do, so it never promises a feature that isn't there. Minecraft, Bedrock, Valheim, Terraria, Rust, ARK, ARK: Survival Ascended, CS2 and Palworld have their own tours. Every other game gets a general one that follows the same rules. There are also VPS, hosting and domain tours. There's no email tour yet.

**Checks so far:** the typecheck passed and the 18 unit tests passed, but both ran before I added the domain tour. A re-run on the final code is still waiting in the queue.

**Still to do, in order:**
1. Re-run the typecheck and unit tests on the final code.
2. Run the prepared browser test (`.tour-e2e/run.sh`). It checks auto-start, replay, skip and Esc, second-server behaviour, admin viewing, phone layout, keyboard-only use, reduced motion and missing elements, and takes screenshots.
3. Delete the throwaway database and the temporary test files; neither is committed.

**For merging:** the work is on `feature/guided-first-run-tours` in `/opt/nxeon-wt-tours`, commit `e913fcdd00`. It touches about a dozen shared panel files, nearly all with a one-attribute change, plus mounts on the server, hosting and domain pages. The full file list is in the handback report. It adds one new database table (`UserTourProgress`) and changes nothing existing; production needs the schema push at deploy. The step-by-step progress note, including exact commands, is in `/root/agent-notes/tours.md`.
